questions.statement: What is the main contrast in this text?
questions.context: Text: 'While cycling is cheaper than driving, it does not solve the problem of long journeys. Buses cover those distances better, although they run less often than cars leave the parking area.'

options.text: Cycling is inexpensive but unsuitable for long distances
options.feedback: The text pairs the advantage of cycling with its limitation, which is the contrast the whole sentence set builds.

options.text: Buses are more frequent than cars
options.feedback: The text states that buses run less often, which is the opposite of this claim.

options.text: Cars are cheaper than buses
options.feedback: Cost is never compared between cars and buses in the text.

options.text: Parking is easier for cyclists than for drivers
options.feedback: The amount of parking at the destination is mentioned, but nothing compares its convenience.

questions.explanation:
Comparison texts place two items side by side and mark the dimension along which they differ. Naming the dimension, here cost against suitability, is what makes a summary of such a text usable.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which contrastive marker appears in the text?
questions.context: Text: 'The two species share a similar body shape. However, one feeds on fruit while the other hunts small animals.'

options.text: However
options.feedback: 'However' introduces a contrast between two feeding habits after a sentence establishing similarity.

options.text: Therefore
options.feedback: 'Therefore' introduces a consequence and would not signal opposition.

options.text: For example
options.feedback: 'For example' introduces an illustration of the point just made.

options.text: As a result
options.feedback: 'As a result' introduces a result, which is not the relation between the two clauses.

questions.explanation:
A short comparison text has a fixed shape: establish what is shared, then mark what differs. The connector tells the reader which relation the following clause carries.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most accurate summary of the comparison?
questions.context: Text: 'The morning market opens earlier but attracts fewer visitors. The afternoon market opens later and draws larger crowds, though the two charge the same prices for produce.'

options.text: The markets differ in hours and in numbers of visitors but not in price
options.feedback: The option captures both stated differences and the one stated similarity in prices.

options.text: The morning market is cheaper and busier than the afternoon one
options.feedback: The prices are the same, and the morning market has fewer visitors rather than more.

options.text: The two markets are identical in every respect
options.feedback: The markets clearly differ in opening hours and in attendance.

options.text: The afternoon market opens earlier and charges more
options.feedback: The afternoon market opens later and prices are equal, so both halves of the last option are wrong.

questions.explanation:
Summarising a comparison requires checking each dimension separately. A summary is accurate only when every attribute it mentions matches the text.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the word 'Unlike' signal?
questions.context: Text: 'Unlike the previous version, this one runs on a battery, and it is also smaller and lighter.'

options.text: A difference from the version being compared with
options.feedback: 'Unlike' sets this version apart from the previous one, which is the function of the word.

options.text: A similarity between the two versions
options.feedback: A similarity would be introduced by 'like' or 'similarly'.

options.text: A cause of one of the differences
options.feedback: No causal relation is expressed between the versions.

options.text: A comparison of prices
options.feedback: Price is not mentioned in the sentence.

questions.explanation:
Prefixes such as 'un', 'dis' and 'con' carry the meaning of the word they begin. Knowing the family of contrastive connectors is a fast route to identifying the relation a sentence expresses.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the comparison show?
questions.context: Text: 'Both schools introduced the reading programme. One school saw scores rise in every year of the study. The other saw a rise in the first year only, followed by a plateau.'

options.text: The effect of the programme was sustained in one school but not in the other
options.feedback: Continuous gains and an initial rise followed by a plateau are different patterns, so the durability of the effect differed.

options.text: The programme failed in both schools
options.feedback: One school improved throughout, so a claim of failure everywhere is wrong.

options.text: The programme succeeded in both schools
options.feedback: The second school's result plateaued, which is not the same as sustained success.

options.text: The schools had identical results
options.feedback: The two patterns are clearly not identical.

questions.explanation:
When two cases share a treatment, the difference in outcome points at whatever else differed between them. Reporting the pattern accurately is the first step in explaining it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this text do to the two options?
questions.context: Text: 'City buses cover the whole network but take longer than the train. The train, on the other hand, serves only two lines, so many passengers must still travel by bus at one end of the journey.'

options.text: It presents each as strong on one dimension and weak on another, leaving the choice open
options.feedback: Coverage and speed are given as advantages of different options, so neither is presented as simply better.

options.text: It declares the bus the better option without qualification
options.feedback: The advantage of the train over the bus is stated explicitly, which rules out an unqualified verdict for buses.

options.text: It claims that the two options are equivalent
options.feedback: The text states differences rather than equivalence.

options.text: It shows that the train serves the whole network
options.feedback: The train is said to serve only two lines, which is the opposite of the last option.

questions.explanation:
A balanced comparison text is one where each option wins on a different axis. Recognising that structure stops a reader from reading a recommendation where the writer offered a trade-off.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the word 'however' do in the second sentence?
questions.context: Text: 'Both methods achieve the same result on small samples. On samples of five hundred or more, however, the second method proves consistently more accurate.'

options.text: It marks a limit to the similarity established in the first sentence
options.feedback: The contrast shows that agreement on small samples does not extend to larger ones.

options.text: It confirms the similarity with further examples
options.feedback: A confirming marker would be 'indeed' or 'likewise', not 'however'.

options.text: It introduces a reason for the similarity
options.feedback: No causal link between the two samples is asserted.

options.text: It summarises both sentences
options.feedback: A summary would gather the content rather than oppose it.

questions.explanation:
A contrast inside a comparison often appears at the exact point where the parallel breaks down. Reading for that point tells a reader where the rule stops applying.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which comparison does this text make between the two systems?
questions.context: Text: 'The old system processes a request in four hours. The new system processes the same request in ninety minutes, which is roughly two and a half times faster.'

options.text: It compares duration and expresses the improvement as a ratio
options.feedback: Both figures are times, and the ratio between four hours and ninety minutes is the basis of the comparison.

options.text: It compares cost and expresses the improvement as a percentage
options.feedback: No cost figure appears in the text at all.

options.text: It compares reliability and expresses the improvement as a margin
options.feedback: Accuracy and error margins are not discussed.

options.text: It compares popularity and expresses the improvement as a ranking
options.feedback: No measure of popularity is mentioned.

questions.explanation:
Quantitative comparisons name their dimension explicitly. Confirming that the same unit appears on both sides of a comparison prevents a reader from accepting a ratio computed from unrelated figures.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the text mention two different measures of biodiversity?
questions.context: Text: 'The dry forest lost more species than the wet forest, yet it recovered faster after the drought ended. One measure of diversity fell while another measure of abundance rose.'

options.text: To show that the answer depends on which measure is used
options.feedback: When two valid measures point in opposite directions, a single verdict depends on the reader's choice of indicator.

options.text: To demonstrate that the two forests are identical
options.feedback: The text reports different results, which is the opposite of identity.

options.text: To suggest that one of the measurements was wrong
options.feedback: Nothing suggests that any measurement was faulty.

options.text: To prove that the wet forest is richer in every respect
options.feedback: The dry forest recovered faster, so the last option does not follow.

questions.explanation:
Noticing that a comparison uses different measures on each side is a frequent route to a well-founded criticism. It also explains why two experts can disagree about the same data.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the text caution against?
questions.context: Text: 'The comparison with last year is not exact, since the boundaries of the area were redrawn in March. Figures before and after March therefore cover different territory.'

options.text: Treating figures from the two periods as directly comparable
options.feedback: Different areas in the two periods mean the counts are not measuring the same thing.

options.text: Publishing any figures for the year
options.feedback: The caution is about comparability, and the text still supplies figures for the year.

options.text: Redrawing the boundaries again
options.feedback: No suggestion to change the boundaries appears in the passage.

options.text: Using the figures from after March only
options.feedback: Discarding the later figures would remove the very period the text is discussing.

questions.explanation:
A change of measurement boundaries is a technical version of the comparability problem. Texts often state this in a footnote, and a reader who notices it can avoid repeating the author's conclusion.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this comparison allow a reader to conclude?
questions.context: Text: 'Both schools were given the same materials and the same training. The school that received three extra teaching hours a week improved more than twice as much as the school that did not.'

options.text: The extra teaching hours were the main factor associated with the larger gain
options.feedback: With materials and training held constant, the one varying feature is the extra hours, so the difference points to them.

options.text: The school with better teaching is always more successful
options.feedback: A general claim about teaching quality is broader than a comparison between two schools.

options.text: The materials were of no use in either school
options.feedback: Both schools received the same materials, so their value is untested rather than shown to be nil.

options.text: Three hours a week is the ideal amount of teaching everywhere
options.feedback: One instance cannot establish an ideal amount for every school.

questions.explanation:
A comparison becomes informative when the compared cases share everything except the factor under examination. Identifying that shared background is what makes the difference meaningful.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the final section?
questions.context: Text: 'The report compares two models of rural transport. It presents each in turn, then ends with a short section weighing the practical factors rather than declaring a winner.'

options.text: To evaluate both options using stated criteria without selecting one
options.feedback: Weighing stated factors while declining to choose is the standard form of an evaluative conclusion in a comparison.

options.text: To announce the better option after presenting both
options.feedback: A declared winner is explicitly excluded by the description.

options.text: To repeat the description of the first model
options.feedback: The final section evaluates rather than redescribes.

options.text: To explain how the two models were built
options.feedback: Construction details belong to an earlier section, and the described final section does not address them.

questions.explanation:
Comparison texts often end with an evaluative section that applies criteria to both options. Knowing whether the writer declares a winner tells a reader how much weight to give the text's overall stance.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most accurate reading of the text?
questions.context: Text: 'Option A costs less and takes longer. Option B costs more and takes less time. The deciding factor for most users was neither price nor speed but comfort.'

options.text: The stated pairwise contrasts are accurate, and a third factor decides the choice
options.feedback: The two sentences form a consistent cost and speed trade-off, and the last sentence adds a criterion outside it.

options.text: The text is self-contradictory because it gives two comparisons
options.feedback: Two comparisons of different dimensions are consistent rather than contradictory.

options.text: The text argues that comfort matters more than price and speed
options.feedback: The text reports how users decided rather than arguing that comfort should dominate.

options.text: The text shows that price and speed are the only criteria considered
options.feedback: The final sentence explicitly introduces a factor beyond price and speed.

questions.explanation:
A report can present a clean trade-off on two dimensions and then note that users weighed something else. Recognising the third criterion prevents a reader from reducing the text to its first two sentences.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the concessive clause contribute?
questions.context: Text: 'Compared with the model trained on one site, the model trained on four sites performed better everywhere, although the margin was small at the fourth site itself.'

options.text: It acknowledges the one case where the advantage was least, which strengthens the claim
options.feedback: Noting the smallest margin where the gain is smallest shows the writer checked the claim in every case rather than selecting favourable ones.

options.text: It undermines the claim by showing that the model failed at one site
options.feedback: A small margin is still an advantage and does not amount to failure.

options.text: It explains why the first model was replaced
options.feedback: Nothing in the sentence explains why one model was replaced.

options.text: It reports a statistical test that failed
options.feedback: No statistical test is mentioned anywhere in the text.

questions.explanation:
A concession that reports the least favourable case is a sign of thorough analysis rather than a weakness. This item asks the student to read a limiting statement as evidence about the writer's method.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What criticism does this text invite?
questions.context: Text: 'The text compares the two languages twice: first by vocabulary, then by word order. Between those two comparisons the text changes what the words mean without announcing it.'

options.text: The two comparisons may not be based on the same meaning of the term, so they may not be comparable
options.feedback: If the defining terms shift between the two comparisons, the results belong to different questions and cannot simply be set beside each other.

options.text: The second comparison is too long to be read carefully
options.feedback: Length is a reading concern rather than a logical defect in the comparison.

options.text: The text repeats the same evidence twice
options.feedback: Repetition would be a stylistic issue and is not described here.

options.text: The text should have used more technical vocabulary
options.feedback: Technical vocabulary is not a requirement of a valid comparison.

questions.explanation:
Consistency of definitions across a comparison is what makes its parts comparable. This item targets the idea that two analyses are only additive if they answer the same question.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the comparison establish and what does it leave open?
questions.context: Text: 'The new law resembles one introduced in another country, but the other country applied it for only two years. Here it has already been in force for six.'

options.text: It establishes that the legal texts are similar and leaves open whether the longer application has worked better
options.feedback: The similarity of the legal texts is stated, and the difference in duration is given without any outcome evidence.

options.text: It establishes that the policy has succeeded here because it worked elsewhere
options.feedback: A comparison of texts says nothing about results, since no outcome from the other country is reported.

options.text: It shows that the two countries chose the law for the same reasons
options.feedback: No reasons for either decision appear in the text.

options.text: It establishes that the law will work better in this country
options.feedback: Nothing in the passage predicts future performance here.

questions.explanation:
Textual similarity and practical result are different things. This item asks the student to say what a comparison establishes and to refuse the additional inference that usually gets attached to it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How does the text contrast the two seasons?
questions.context: Text: 'Unlike the dry season, the wet season does not begin all at once across the province. In the north it arrives three weeks before it does in the south.'

options.text: By contrasting uniformity with variation across the province
options.feedback: The dry season is treated as starting uniformly while the wet season varies by region, and that difference is the contrast being drawn.

options.text: By contrasting the wet season with the dry season
options.feedback: The dry season appears only as the reference point for the wet one, not as the second item of the contrast.

options.text: By contrasting the north with the south
options.feedback: The regional difference is a detail within the wet season rather than the contrast itself.

options.text: By contrasting the length of the two seasons
options.feedback: No duration of either season is given anywhere in the text.

questions.explanation:
A contrast can run between an expected pattern and the actual one rather than between two named items. This item asks the student to locate the real axis of comparison, which is not always the pair of named subjects.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What can a careful reader legitimately conclude from this text?
questions.context: Text: 'Compared with last year, three more families used the clinic. In that same period the number of staff at the clinic rose by one. The text presents these two numbers side by side without comment.'

options.text: That demand and staffing both rose, and that the text does not say whether they rose together
options.feedback: Two figures presented without comment permit only a description of both, not a relation between them.

options.text: That the clinic became badly understaffed during the period
options.feedback: Both figures rose, so a claim of understaffing is not supported.

options.text: That the additional family was caused by the new member of staff
options.feedback: A causal link in that direction requires evidence the text does not supply.

options.text: That staffing levels are unrelated to demand
options.feedback: The text neither establishes nor denies a relationship, and it certainly does not state one.

questions.explanation:
Placing two numbers side by side suggests a connection that the text never asserts. Naming what a passage leaves unsaid is as precise a reading skill as naming what it says.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What type of contrast is presented?
questions.context: Text: 'Both versions of the app allow users to save their work. The free version restricts saving to five items, while the paid version places no limit at all.'

options.text: A quantitative contrast within a shared feature
options.feedback: Both share the same feature, and the difference is the numerical limit applied to it.

options.text: A contrast between two entirely different applications
options.feedback: The two versions perform the same function and differ only in detail, so they are not different applications.

options.text: A temporal contrast between an earlier and a later version
options.feedback: No dates or order of release appear in the text.

options.text: A contrast of tone between the two versions
options.feedback: Nothing in the passage concerns tone or writing style.

questions.explanation:
Comparisons are not only between different things but often between degrees of the same thing. This item checks whether a reader can see a shared feature before measuring the difference.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which criticism of the review is most accurate?
questions.context: Text: 'A review of two films, each described at length and praised in similar terms, concludes: 'The difference between them is negligible.'

options.text: The conclusion follows from the praise but ignores any difference between the two cases
options.feedback: If both films are described almost identically, no dimension has been offered on which one could differ.

options.text: The review praises two films and therefore cannot be balanced
options.feedback: Describing two films in similar terms is exactly what supports the conclusion, so it is not a criticism of balance.

options.text: The review should have chosen one film instead of describing both
options.feedback: A comparison requires both cases to be described, and the review does that.

options.text: The word 'negligible' is not an acceptable English word
options.feedback: 'Negligible' is a standard English word meaning too small to matter.

questions.explanation: A conclusion of equivalence is only supported when a text shows what was compared. This final item asks the student to test whether the stated comparison had any basis at all.
